question: There are a few pixels of empty space between the bottom of the image and the bottom border of `.card`. What causes it?

options.text: Browsers give `` a default `margin-bottom`.
options.why: The UA stylesheet sets no margin on ``. In DevTools the image's margin is 0; the gap is inside `.card`'s content box, below the image.

options.text: The newline after the `` tag in the HTML is rendered as an extra line of text under the image.
options.why: Collapsible whitespace at the end of a line is removed, and even if it weren't, it would sit on the same line as the image, not on a new line. The gap appears even when the markup has no whitespace at all.

options.text: The image is an inline element sitting on the text baseline, and the line box reserves space below the baseline for descenders.
`<div>` has a default `padding-bottom` in the UA stylesheet.
options.why: `<div>` has no default padding or margin. The space comes from the line box the image sits in, which is why changing the image's `display` or `vertical-align` removes it.

explanation: `` is an inline-level (replaced) element, so it sits in a line box like a letter would. With the default `vertical-align: baseline`, its bottom edge sits on the text baseline. Every line box also contains a "strut": an invisible, zero-width inline box with the parent's font and line-height. The strut extends below the baseline (room for descenders like g, j, p, y), so the line box ends a few pixels below the image. That space is the gap. (This is standards-mode behavior. A page without `` renders in quirks mode, where this gap usually doesn't appear, so include the doctype when you try it yourself.) Fixes: - `img { display: block; }` (the image no longer sits in a line box) - `img { vertical-align: top; }` or `bottom` (`middle` often works too, but not always) - make the parent a flex or grid container (the image becomes a blockified item) - `line-height: 0` on the parent (works, but affects any text in it)

question: An icon sits next to a label on the same line. With `vertical-align: middle`, what exactly is the image's vertical midpoint aligned to?

snippets.code: Saved

options.text: The vertical center of the line box
options.why: That's what most people expect, but `middle` is defined relative to the parent's baseline and x-height, not the line box. If a taller element makes the line box taller, a `middle`-aligned image doesn't move to the new center. (`top` and `bottom` are the values that use the line box.)

options.text: The parent's baseline, raised by half the parent's x-height
The center of the text's content area, halfway between the ascender and descender lines
options.why: `middle` doesn't use the text's content area (ascent + descent) or the em box. It uses the baseline plus half the x-height (the height of a lowercase "x"), which is lower than the center of capital letters. That's why a `middle`-aligned icon can look 1–2px low next to capitalized text.

options.text: The midpoint of the tallest inline element on the line
options.why: No `vertical-align` value aligns to a sibling's midpoint. `middle` only looks at the parent's baseline and x-height.

explanation:
The spec (and MDN) define `vertical-align: middle` as: align the vertical midpoint of the box with the baseline of the parent box **plus half the x-height of the parent**.

In most fonts the x-height is roughly half the font size, so the image's center lands about a quarter of an em above the baseline. That's close to the visual middle of lowercase text, but not of capitals, and it ignores the line box entirely.

For predictable centering that ignores baselines, use `display: flex; align-items: center;` on the parent. The icon is then centered against the text's line box (its `line-height` height), not against the glyphs themselves, so depending on the font it can still look slightly off and need a small nudge.

question: The toast should stay pinned to the bottom-right corner of the viewport, but it doesn't. The page is long enough to scroll. Where does the toast actually end up?

options.text: At the bottom-right of the viewport, as intended; `transform` doesn't affect fixed descendants
options.why: It does. Any `transform` other than `none` makes the element the containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.

options.text: 16px in from the bottom-right corner of `.panel`'s padding box, scrolling with the page
Relative to the initial containing block, because there's no positioned ancestor, so it scrolls with the document
options.why: "Nearest positioned ancestor, else the initial containing block" is the rule for `position: absolute`. Fixed elements normally use the viewport, but here the transformed `.panel` takes over that role.

options.text: At the bottom-right of the viewport, but painted underneath `.panel`, because `transform` creates a stacking context
options.why: `transform` does create a stacking context, but that only affects painting order. The bigger effect is on the containing block: the toast no longer stays at the viewport corner at all.

explanation:
A `position: fixed` element is normally positioned relative to the viewport. But if an ancestor has a `transform` other than `none` (even an identity transform like `translateX(0)`), that ancestor becomes the containing block for its fixed and absolute descendants. The offsets are then measured from the ancestor's padding box, and the element scrolls along with it.

The same happens with `filter`, `perspective`, `will-change: transform`, and `contain: paint`, among others. This often bites modals and toasts rendered inside animated containers.

Fix: render the fixed element outside the transformed ancestor (for example at the end of `<body>`, or with a React portal).

question: The paragraph wraps onto three lines, and the 48px image is at the start of the first line. With `line-height: 20px`, how is the paragraph laid out?

snippets.code: Long welcome text that wraps onto three lines in this narrow box...

options.text: Every line is spaced 20px apart; the image overflows its line and overlaps the text of the line above it, because `line-height` is a fixed length
options.why: `line-height` sets the height of each *inline box's* contribution, not a hard cap on the line box. The line box grows to contain the image's full height, so nothing overlaps.

options.text: All three lines become about 48px tall, because the paragraph's line height is raised to fit its tallest content
options.why: Line boxes are sized independently. Only the line that actually contains the image grows; the following lines are still 20px apart.

options.text: Only the first line box grows tall enough to contain the image; the second and third lines are still 20px apart
The text wraps beside the image like a float, filling the 48px next to it with two or three short lines
options.why: That's `float: left` behavior. An inline image is just a tall item on one line; the text after it continues on that same line and then wraps below it, not alongside it.

explanation:
Each line box is as tall as needed to contain all the inline boxes on **that line**: from the highest top to the lowest bottom, after `vertical-align` is applied.

On the first line, the image is baseline-aligned, so it extends 48px above the baseline. The line box stretches from the image's top down to the bottom of the strut (a little below the baseline), making the first line noticeably taller than 20px. The text on that line sits at the bottom, next to the image's lower edge.

The second and third lines contain only text, so they keep the 20px spacing. The result is uneven spacing: a big first line, then normal lines.

If that looks wrong, the fix is usually to take the image out of the line: `float` it, use `display: block`, or put the image and text in a flex/grid layout.

options.text: Nothing changes, because `line-height` only affects text and the card has no text
options.why: Every line box has a strut, an invisible zero-width box with the parent's font and `line-height`. The strut is there even with no text, so changing `line-height` changes the line box.

options.text: The gap disappears, because the taller line height now fits around the image
options.why: A bigger `line-height` makes the strut taller, not shorter. The image is still on the baseline, and the strut now reaches even further below it.

options.text: The card grows, but the extra space is added above the image, so the gap below stays the same
options.why: Leading is split evenly above and below the text. The part above stays inside the 40px of image that is already above the baseline, so the card only grows at the bottom.

options.text: The gap grows, because half of the extra leading is added below the strut's baseline

explanation:
The image sits on the baseline. Below the baseline, the line box extends to the bottom of the **strut**: the font's descent **plus half the leading** (leading = `line-height` minus the font's content height).

Raising `line-height` from `1.2` (19.2px) to `2` (32px) adds about 13px of leading, half of it below the baseline. The exact gap depends on the font's descent: with a 16px Times New Roman or Arial it goes from about 4px to about 11px, with Segoe UI from about 3px to 10px. Whatever the font, it grows by roughly that half (about 6.4px). The half added above doesn't show, because the 40px image already reaches higher than the strut.

So on rows that mix images and text, `line-height` can make the image look like it has a big bottom margin. Fixes that ignore `line-height` entirely: `img { display: block; }`, `img { vertical-align: top; }` (for an image taller than the line), or making the parent a flex/grid container.

question: A heading uses an emoji in one place and a `1em × 1em` image icon in another, both at the default `vertical-align`. Which statement best describes how each is positioned vertically?

options.text: Both sit with their bottom edge exactly on the baseline, because the browser renders an emoji as a small inline image
options.why: Color emoji look like pictures, but in layout they are ordinary text glyphs from an emoji font. Like any glyph, they're placed by font metrics, and most emoji fonts draw them partly below the baseline.

options.text: Both are centered in the line box, because emoji and images are both atomic inline content
options.why: Nothing on an inline line is centered by default; the default is `baseline`. And an emoji isn't an atomic inline box at all: it's a character in a text run.

options.text: Both are automatically aligned to the x-height midpoint, as if `vertical-align: middle` were set, because emoji fonts and SVG icons are designed for it
options.why: Neither is aligned by `middle` unless you set it. The image's default is `baseline` (bottom edge on the baseline), and the emoji is placed by its font's metrics like any letter.

options.text: The image's bottom edge sits exactly on the baseline; the emoji is a text glyph positioned by its font's metrics, and typically dips below the baseline like a descender

explanation: The two follow different rules: - The `` is an atomic inline box with no baseline of its own, so its **bottom edge** goes on the baseline. That's guaranteed by the spec. - The emoji is a **character**. It's drawn from an emoji font (often via font fallback) and positioned like any letter: its baseline matches the text baseline, and the glyph's artwork extends wherever the font designer put it. In common emoji fonts (Segoe UI Emoji on Windows, for example) the picture reaches below the baseline, so it sits lower than a baseline-aligned image. The exact offset varies by font and OS. Consequences: - You can't apply `vertical-align` to a bare emoji character; wrap it in a `` first. - Font fallback to an emoji font can also make that line a bit taller than the others. - Icon fonts (``) behave the same way as emoji: they are glyphs, so they follow `font-size`, `color` and the font's own metrics, not image rules. To make images and glyph icons line up consistently, size them in `em` and nudge them explicitly (for example `vertical-align: -0.125em`), or use a flex row with `align-items: center`.

Its top lines up with the top of the name's text, as intended
options.why: That's `vertical-align: text-top`, which aligns with the top of the parent's content area (the font's ascent). `top` aligns with the top of the whole **line box**, and here the avatar makes the line box much taller than the text.

options.text: It's vertically centered next to the avatar, because `top` is relative to the tallest element's midpoint
options.why: No `vertical-align` value uses another element's midpoint. `top` uses the top edge of the line box, which here is the avatar's top edge.

options.text: It doesn't move: `top` has no effect when another element on the line is taller

The values that track the text instead are:
- `text-top` / `text-bottom`: the top/bottom of the parent's font content area
- `middle`: the parent's baseline + half its x-height
- a length like `-0.125em` or a percentage: an offset from the baseline (negative lowers the box)

- or increase `line-height` on the paragraph so the lines are far enough apart to fit the padding.

options.text: Nothing at all: margins don't apply to inline elements.

options.text: Three lines: "Before", then the div spanning the full 500px width, then "after". The span is split into an inline piece before the div and another after it.
The HTML parser closes the `<span>` before the `<div>`, so the div and "after" end up outside the span and get no red border.

In the DOM the div is still a child of the span: `span.getClientRects()` even returns three rectangles in Chrome, the middle one being the div's area. topic: text-align and block vs inline-block children
question: The word "Card" is centered, but the 200px card itself stays at the left edge of `.wrap`. Why?

options.text: `text-align` isn't inherited, so it can't affect the card at all.
options.why: `text-align` is inherited; that's exactly why the word "Card" is centered inside the card.

options.text: `text-align` aligns inline-level content inside line boxes. The card is a block box, so it isn't positioned by it; it only inherits the value and centers its own text.
`.wrap` needs an explicit `width` before `text-align: center` can center anything inside it.
options.why: A block with `width: auto` already has a definite width (it fills its container). The problem is that `text-align` doesn't move block children at all, whatever the parent's width.

options.text: A fixed `width` turns off centering; with `width: auto` the card would be centered.
options.why: With `width: auto` the block card would simply fill the whole row, so there would be nothing to center. Its fixed width is fine; it just needs a different centering mechanism.

explanation:
`text-align` is a property of the block container: it says how inline-level content (text, inline and inline-block boxes, images) is distributed within each line box. A `display: block` child is not inside a line box; it's laid out in block flow and starts at the container's start edge. Because `text-align` is inherited, the card's own line of text is centered, which is the confusing part.

Fixes:
- Center the block itself: `.card { margin-inline: auto; }` (works because it has a width narrower than the container).
- Or make it inline-level: `.card { display: inline-block; }`. Now it sits in `.wrap`'s line box, and `text-align: center` centers it.
- Or use flex/grid on `.wrap` (`display: grid; justify-items: center;` or `display: flex; justify-content: center;`).

question: The tag's text is long enough to wrap, so the span is split across two lines. With the default `box-decoration-break` value, where is the 12px horizontal padding (and the border on the left and right sides) drawn?

snippets.code: Tags: aaaa bbbb cccc dddd eeee ffff gggg end

options.text: On both the left and right side of each line's piece, so each piece looks like a complete tag.
options.why: That's what `box-decoration-break: clone` does. The initial value is `slice`, which renders the box as if it were one long box cut at the line break.

options.text: Nowhere: horizontal padding is ignored when an inline element wraps.
options.why: Horizontal padding on inline boxes always applies. Wrapping only changes which fragment gets it; you can see the extra space before "cccc" and after "gggg".

options.text: Only at the start of the first line's piece and the end of the second line's piece; the edges at the line break are open, with no border or padding.
At the left edge of each line's piece, and at the right edge only on the last piece.
options.why: Fragments don't get the start edge repeated per line. With `slice`, the start padding/border appears once (on the first fragment) and the end padding/border once (on the last).

explanation:
An inline box that wraps is split into one fragment per line. With the initial `box-decoration-break: slice`, the fragments are treated as slices of one continuous box: the start-side padding, border and margin go only on the first fragment, the end-side ones only on the last, and the edges at the break have none. The background is also drawn as if over the whole unbroken box.

`box-decoration-break: clone` decorates each fragment independently: each gets its own left and right padding and border (and its own `border-radius`, `box-shadow` and background). This is handy for multi-line highlighted text or tags.

You can measure it: `span.getClientRects()` returns one rect per fragment, and with `clone` each rect grows by the padding plus border of the side that was missing.

Support note: Chrome and Firefox support the unprefixed property; Safari needs `-webkit-box-decoration-break`, so write both.

Horizontal margins follow the same slice rule: `margin-left` appears only before the first fragment and `margin-right` only after the last.

question: Both chips contain the same empty `<span class="icon">` with a fixed size. In which chip is the 16 × 16 icon square actually visible?

snippets.code: Save Save

options.text: In both chips, because inline-block and inline-flex both turn their children into block-level boxes.
options.why: `inline-block` only changes the chip's outer behavior and makes it a block container. Its children are still laid out in normal flow, so the `<span>` stays inline and ignores `width`/`height`.

options.text: In neither chip, because a `<span>` is inline and inline elements ignore `width` and `height`.
options.why: True inside the inline-block chip, but not inside the inline-flex one: children of a flex container are flex items, and flex items are blockified (`display: block`), so they honor `width` and `height`.

options.text: Only in the inline-block chip, because inline-flex shrinks empty flex items to zero width.
options.why: An empty flex item isn't sized from its content when it has an explicit `width`: `width: 16px` becomes its flex base size, and the inline-flex chip sizes itself to fit its items, so there's no pressure to shrink. It renders at 16 × 16.

options.text: Only in the inline-flex chip: its children become flex items and are blockified, while inside the inline-block chip the span stays inline and its width and height are ignored.

explanation:
`inline-block` and `inline-flex` have the same **outer** display: both sit in a line like a word, don't force line breaks, and honor their own `width`/`height`. They differ in their **inner** display, which decides how their children are laid out:

- `inline-block` (= `inline flow-root`): children use normal block/inline flow. An empty inline `<span>` has zero width there, so the icon isn't visible.
- `inline-flex` (= `inline flex`): children become flex items. Flex items are blockified, so `getComputedStyle(icon).display` becomes `block` and the 16 × 16 size applies.

To show the icon inside the inline-block chip, give the icon itself `display: inline-block` (and usually a `vertical-align`), or switch the chip to `inline-flex` as in the second chip.

question: CSS Display Level 3 splits `display` into an outer display type (how the box takes part in its parent's layout) and an inner display type (how it lays out its children). Which multi-keyword value is equivalent to `display: inline-block`?

options.text: `display: inline flow`
options.why: `flow` means "normal flow, with no new formatting context". `inline flow` is just `display: inline`: an ordinary inline box whose width and height are ignored.

options.text: `display: inline flow-root`
`display: inline block`
options.why: `block` is an outer display type, not an inner one, so it can't be combined with `inline`. The declaration is invalid and is dropped, leaving the previous `display` value in place.

options.text: `display: block flow-root`
options.why: That's the same as `display: flow-root`: a block-level box that starts on its own line and establishes a new block formatting context. The outer type is `block`, so it doesn't sit inside a line.

explanation:
The outer type is `inline` (the box sits inside a line box, like a word) and the inner type is `flow-root` (it lays out its contents in normal flow and establishes a new block formatting context, so it has its own size, contains floats, and its children's margins don't collapse through it). That's exactly what `inline-block` is.

The legacy single keywords map to pairs:
- `block` = `block flow`
- `inline` = `inline flow`
- `inline-block` = `inline flow-root`
- `flow-root` = `block flow-root`
- `inline-flex` = `inline flex`, `inline-grid` = `inline grid`

You can check it in the browser: `CSS.supports('display', 'inline flow-root')` is `true`, and after setting it, `getComputedStyle(el).display` reports `"inline-block"` (the shortest serialization). `CSS.supports('display', 'inline block')` is `false`.

question: The icon should be vertically centered in the 48px toolbar, but it sits at the top edge. Why doesn't `vertical-align: middle` do anything here?

options.why: That's the old single-line centering trick for inline content: a tall `line-height` makes a tall line box for the content to sit in. The icon isn't in a line box here, so adding `line-height: 48px` to `.toolbar` leaves it at the top. Only the text inside the `<span>` moves.

options.text: `` is a replaced element. Adding `display: inline-block` to the icon makes `vertical-align` apply.
options.why: Children of a flex container are blockified: whatever `display` you give them computes to a block-level value (`inline-block` becomes `block`). The icon is still a flex item and still ignores `vertical-align`.

options.text: The icon is a flex item, and `vertical-align` has no effect on flex items. Cross-axis position comes from `align-items` / `align-self`.
`vertical-align` has to go on the container: `.toolbar { vertical-align: middle; }`.

explanation: `vertical-align` only applies to **inline-level boxes** (it positions them inside a line box) and to **table cells**. The Flexbox spec says it plainly: `vertical-align` has no effect on a flex item. The icon is a direct child of a flex container, so it's a flex item. Its `display` is blockified (DevTools shows the computed `display` of the `` as `block`), and it isn't placed in a line box at all, so there's nothing for `vertical-align` to align it against. The icon sits at the top because `align-items` defaults to `normal`, which acts like `stretch` for flex items, and an item with a fixed height can't stretch, so it stays at the cross-start edge. Fix it with flexbox alignment: - `.toolbar { align-items: center; }` (centers every item) - or `.toolbar .icon { align-self: center; }` (just the icon)

question: `.stack` is an inline-block with three lines of text, sitting on the same line as the word "Label" with the default `vertical-align: baseline`. Which part of `.stack` lines up with the baseline of "Label"?

options.text: The baseline of "Line one", so the box hangs down below "Label"
options.why: That's how flexbox and grid `align-items: baseline` work (they use the first baseline by default). An inline-block's baseline in inline layout is the baseline of its **last** line box, not its first.

options.text: The bottom border edge of the box sits on the baseline
options.why: An inline-block only uses its bottom margin edge as its baseline when it has no in-flow line boxes (it's empty) or its `overflow` isn't `visible`. This one has visible overflow and three lines of text.

options.text: The vertical center of the box lines up with the middle of "Label"
options.why: Nothing here asks for centering. Even `vertical-align: middle` would use the parent's baseline plus half its x-height, not the middle of the text. With the default `baseline`, a baseline inside the box is matched to the parent's baseline.

options.text: The baseline of "Line three", so the box extends upward above "Label"

explanation:
With `vertical-align: baseline`, an inline-block is placed so that **its** baseline sits on the parent's baseline. CSS 2 defines an inline-block's baseline as the baseline of its **last line box** in normal flow.

Here the last line box holds "Line three", so "Line three" and "Label" share a baseline. The first two lines and the top padding/border stick up above the text, and the line box grows upward to fit them. In Chrome, the bottoms of inline `<span>`s around "Label" and "Line three" measure exactly equal.

Two exceptions use the bottom margin edge instead: an inline-block with no in-flow line boxes, and one whose `overflow` is not `visible`.

question: Before `overflow: hidden` was added (it's needed for the ellipsis), "Status" and "Archived" shared a baseline. Now the tag's text sits a few pixels higher than "Status". Which single change puts the two words back on the same baseline while keeping the `max-width` truncation and the ellipsis? (Current Chrome/Edge.)

options.text: Replace `overflow: hidden` with `overflow-x: hidden; overflow-y: visible;`, so only the horizontal axis is clipped.
options.why: Tempting because the ellipsis only needs horizontal clipping. But when one axis is not `visible`, a `visible` on the other axis computes to `auto`, so the tag is still a scroll container and its baseline is still its bottom margin edge. The text stays raised by the same amount.

options.text: Replace `overflow: hidden` with `overflow: clip`.
Add `line-height: 1` to the tag so its line box is shorter and the text sits lower.
options.why: This shrinks the space under the text's baseline a little, but the tag is still aligned by its bottom edge, not its text, so "Archived" stays raised (in Chrome it's still about 6px high instead of 7px). Changing line height tweaks the gap; it doesn't change which baseline is used.

options.text: Change `display: inline-block` to `display: inline`.
options.why: The words do line up again, but `max-width`, `overflow` and `text-overflow` don't apply to inline boxes, so the tag stops truncating and the ellipsis disappears. That breaks the requirement.

explanation:
Normally an inline-block's baseline is the baseline of its last line box, so the text inside lines up with the text outside. But there's a legacy exception: an inline-block that is a **scroll container** uses its **bottom margin edge** as its baseline. CSS 2.2 words it as "`overflow` is not `visible`"; CSS Box Alignment 3 narrows it to scroll containers. With `overflow: hidden`, the tag's bottom edge sits on the parent's baseline, so the text inside is lifted by the space below its own baseline plus the bottom padding and border.

`overflow: clip` clips just like `hidden` but does **not** make the box a scroll container. So the legacy rule doesn't apply, the tag keeps its text baseline, and `text-overflow: ellipsis` still works because `overflow` isn't `visible`. In Chrome, "Status" and "Archived" measure exactly level with `clip`, and the ellipsis still renders.

Other ways to deal with it:
- `baseline-source: last` on the tag (CSS Inline 3) also opts out of the legacy rule in current Chrome/Edge.
- `vertical-align: top`, `bottom` or `middle` change how the tag is placed, but with vertical padding and a border the text still ends up one to a few pixels off (3px for `top`/`bottom` here, the padding plus border), so they're approximations rather than exact fixes.

question: Both boxes are 48px tall inline-blocks with the default `vertical-align: baseline`. The only difference is that the second one contains a letter. How do they line up? (Default font size 16px, `line-height: normal`.)

Their top and bottom edges line up, with both bottom edges on the baseline.
options.why: Only the empty box uses its bottom edge as its baseline. The box with "A" has a line box, so its baseline is the baseline of the "A", near the top of the box. Matching that to the parent's baseline pushes the box down.

options.text: The empty box sits lower: with no text it has no baseline, so the browser hangs it from the top of the line.
options.why: An inline-block without line boxes doesn't fall back to top alignment. Its baseline is defined as its bottom margin edge, so it sits on the baseline and rises above it.

options.why: Equal heights don't mean equal alignment. With `vertical-align: baseline`, each box is positioned by its own baseline, and the two boxes get their baselines from different places.

explanation:
An inline-block's baseline is the baseline of its last line box. When it has **no in-flow line boxes** (it's empty, or holds only collapsible whitespace), CSS 2 says its baseline is its **bottom margin edge**.

- Empty box: bottom edge (plus any `margin-bottom`) on the parent's baseline, so the whole box rises above the text.
- Box with "A": the "A" is on the parent's baseline. The line sits at the top of the 48px box, so the rest of the box hangs below the line and the line box grows downward to fit it.

This is a common source of "why are my identical boxes staggered?" bugs, for example with placeholder or skeleton tiles that fill in with text later. `vertical-align: top` (or a flex/grid parent) makes the position independent of the content.

- `h2`: inherits `21px` as is, not "1.5em"

options.why: The paragraph does grow to 48px, but the highlight doesn't. An inline element's background covers its content area (based on the font's ascent and descent), not its line-height. The extra leading is invisible space around it.

options.text: The highlight keeps its height, but the paragraph grows to 48px, adding empty space above and below the highlight
Nothing changes, because `line-height` has no effect on inline elements

- The **content area**, sized by the font (ascent + descent). Background and borders are painted here.
- The **inline box**, whose height is the `line-height` (16px × 3 = 48px). Extra space is split evenly above and below as half-leading.

The line box must contain every inline box, so the paragraph grows from 24px to 48px. The highlight doesn't change: the `mark`'s `getBoundingClientRect()` height is the same with or without the rule (about 17px with Chrome's default serif font on Windows; the exact number depends on the font), and it now sits in the middle of a 48px line.

explanation:
`getComputedStyle()` returns **resolved values** (CSSOM). For most properties that's the computed value, but some properties have special rules:

question: When the scroller is wide, the card is centered. When the scroller is narrower than the card (300px vs 500px here), the card's left edge is cut off and you can't scroll back to it. What's going on, and what fixes it?

options.text: `overflow-x: auto` doesn't scroll to content on the left; switch to `overflow-x: scroll`.
options.why: `auto` and `scroll` create the same kind of scroll container; `scroll` only shows the scrollbar all the time. Neither lets you scroll to content that overflows past the start (left) edge, so the problem stays.

options.text: The card can't overflow normally because of its automatic minimum size; add `min-width: 0` to `.card`.
options.why: `min-width` only limits how far an item can **shrink**. The card is `flex: none` and is meant to stay 500px. The problem is where `justify-content` places it, and with `min-width: 0` it still starts at -100px.

options.text: The browser starts the scroller scrolled to the middle; set `scrollLeft = 0` to reveal the left edge.
options.why: `scrollLeft` is already 0 and can't go lower. The hidden 100px sits at a negative offset, outside the scrollable area (`scrollWidth` is 400, not 500).

options.text: `justify-content: center` splits the overflow equally on both sides, and the part past the left edge is unreachable. Use `justify-content: safe center`, or drop `justify-content` and put `margin: 0 auto` on the card.

explanation:
The free space is 300 − 500 = −100px. `justify-content: center` splits it equally, so the card starts at x = −100px relative to the scroller and overflows by 100px on each side.

Scroll containers only let you scroll to overflow on the **end** side (right, in left-to-right text). Overflow past the start edge is clipped for good. In Chrome the scroller's `scrollWidth` is 400px: the right-hand 100px is reachable, the left-hand 100px is not.

Two fixes:
- `justify-content: safe center`: centers while the card fits, falls back to `start` when it would overflow. The card then starts at 0 and `scrollWidth` is 500. `safe` works in flex layout in all current evergreen browsers (Chrome/Edge 115+, Firefox 63+, Safari 17.6+).
- `margin: 0 auto` on the card (and drop `justify-content`). Auto margins center when there is positive free space, but are set to 0 when the free space is negative, so the card overflows only to the right. Dropping `justify-content` matters: if `center` stays, the auto margins are zeroed and `justify-content` centers the overflow again, so the card is back at −100px.

Add `max-width: 100%` to `.table-wrap`.

options.text: Stretching only applies to items whose `height` is `auto`. And 100% of the row's auto height can't be resolved, so the card falls back to its content height.

options.why: `.bar` isn't a flex item; `.body` is an ordinary block container, so nothing stretches `.bar`. Its `height: 50%` resolves against `.body`'s 300px.

explanation:
Normally `height: 50%` needs a containing block with a definite height, and a plain block with `height: auto` doesn't have one. In block layout, `.bar` would be 0px tall.

options.why: The `fr` algorithm doesn't give the other columns their original 200px share. Once a column is held at its minimum, it is treated as fixed and the remaining 300px is re-divided between the other two `1fr` columns.

options.text: 300px, 150px, 150px: the first column can't shrink below the image, and the other two share what's left.
300px, 300px, 300px: `fr` columns must stay equal, so every column grows to the widest one.
options.why: Chrome does produce `300px 300px 300px` when the grid's own width is indefinite, e.g. `display: inline-grid` with no width, because then the `fr` size is found from the content. Here the grid has a definite 600px width, so `fr` shares out that space instead.

explanation:
`1fr` is shorthand for `minmax(auto, 1fr)`. The `auto` minimum is the item's **automatic minimum size**, which for a grid item that isn't a scroll container is its min-content size. The first card can't be narrower than the 300px image inside it, so its track has a 300px minimum.

The `fr` sizing then runs like this:

- First try: 600px / 3 = 200px per `fr`.
- The first track's minimum (300px) is bigger than its 200px share, so it is fixed at 300px and taken out of the calculation.
- The remaining 600 − 300 = 300px is shared by the other two tracks: 150px each.

Chrome reports `grid-template-columns: 300px 150px 150px`, and the grid still fits its 600px width.

To get truly equal columns, remove the content-based minimum:

```css
.cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
```

Chrome then reports `200px 200px 200px`, and the image overflows its card (add `img { max-width: 100%; }` to make it shrink instead). Setting `min-width: 0` or `overflow: hidden` on the cards works too, because both remove the automatic minimum. This is the grid version of the flexbox `min-width: auto` problem.

explanation:

- A goes to row 1, column 1.
- B needs all three columns, which don't fit after A, so it goes to row 2, leaving two holes in row 1.
- C and D go to row 3, columns 1–2.

The grid is 150px tall. With `dense`, each auto-placed item looks for the **first** free spot from the start of the grid, so C and D fill the holes in row 1 (columns 2 and 3). Chrome measures the grid at 100px tall, with B still in row 2.

Only the visual position changes. The DOM order (and the Tab and reading order that follows it) stays A, B, C, D, so a keyboard user will jump around the layout. Use `dense` for things like image galleries, not for items whose order carries meaning.

options.why: Line numbers refer to grid lines, not the container's edges. The tracks here add up to 400px, and the container's leftover 200px isn't part of any track.

options.why: This is the tempting one, but negative numbers count back from the end of the **explicit** grid only. The badge's implicit columns 3 and 4 don't count, so `-1` is line 3.

options.text: 100px: the header and the badge conflict, so the header falls back to a single auto-placed column.

explanation:
`grid-template-columns: 100px 100px` defines an **explicit** grid with two columns, so lines 1, 2 and 3. The badge asks for column 4, so the grid adds **implicit** columns 3 and 4 (100px each, from `grid-auto-columns`). Chrome reports `grid-template-columns: 100px 100px 100px 100px` and places the badge at x = 300px.

Negative line numbers count back from the end edge of the explicit grid only, so `-1` is still line 3. The header spans lines 1–3: 200px wide. Chrome measures exactly that.

To make a header span every column, define all of them explicitly (for example `repeat(4, 100px)`), so that `-1` is the true last line. Positive numbers past the explicit grid (like `4` here) create implicit tracks; negative ones never reach them.

question: The developer wanted the nav to wrap under `main` in an L shape. Instead, the header, nav and main all pile up on top of each other in the same cell, past the right edge of the 200px and 400px columns. Why?

options.text: Only the invalid `side` area is dropped: the nav falls back to auto-placement, but the header and main still go to their named areas.
options.why: Areas aren't validated one by one. The whole declaration is invalid, so Chrome's computed `grid-template-areas` is `none` and the header and main lose their places too, which is why all three items overlap.

options.text: The row strings must be separated by commas, so the value is read as a single row.
options.why: The syntax is one quoted string per row, separated only by whitespace, with no commas. If you make the areas rectangular (e.g. `"side foot"` in the last row), Chrome lays this exact syntax out correctly.

options.text: Every named area must be a single rectangle. The L-shaped `side` makes the whole `grid-template-areas` value invalid, so it's dropped and none of the names exist.
`grid-template-areas` needs a `grid-template-rows` with three row sizes; without it, the areas are ignored.
options.why: Row sizes are optional: the strings themselves define three explicit rows, and they default to `auto`. With rectangular areas, Chrome places all three items correctly without any `grid-template-rows`.

explanation:
Each named area in `grid-template-areas` must form a filled-in rectangle. Here, `side` covers row 2 column 1 plus all of row 3: an L shape. A non-rectangular (or disconnected) area makes the **entire declaration invalid**, and like any invalid CSS it's thrown away at parse time. Chrome reports `grid-template-areas: none`.

With no areas, `grid-area: head` looks for lines named `head-start` and `head-end`, then for lines named plain `head`, and none of them exist. The spec says that when no line has the name, **implicit** grid lines are treated as having it, so the items are placed in implicit tracks after the explicit grid instead of in their intended cells. In Chrome, `grid-template-columns` gains two implicit columns after `200px 400px`, and all three items overlap in the second of them, to the right of the two explicit columns.

Fix: keep every area rectangular. Give the extra cell its own name (or `.` for an empty cell), for example:

```css
grid-template-areas:
  "head head"
  "side main"
  "side foot";
```

With that value, Chrome puts the header across both columns, the nav in column 1 across rows 2–3, and main in row 2, column 2. A real L shape needs two separate elements (or a different layout).

question: How tall is `.list`, and how far from its top edge does the second span start? `.list` has no padding or border.

options.text: Spans are inline, so `height` and vertical margins are ignored: `.list` is two text lines tall.
options.why: That's true for spans in normal flow, but grid items are blockified: Chrome reports `display: block` for the spans, and `height` and the vertical margins both apply.

options.text: 80px tall, and the second span starts at 50px: the margins between the spans collapse into one, and the outer margins collapse through `.list`.
options.why: That's how the same markup behaves in normal block flow, with `display: block` on the spans and no grid. Margins of grid items never collapse, either with each other or with the grid container.

options.text: 120px tall, and the second span starts at 70px: the margins between the spans collapse to 20px, but the outer ones stay inside `.list`.
options.why: Half right: the outer margins do stay inside. But the margins **between** grid items don't collapse either; each item's full margin box sits in its own row.

options.text: 140px tall, and the second span starts at 90px: each span's margin box (20 + 30 + 20) fills its own 70px row, and no margins collapse.

explanation:
Two grid rules apply:

- **Blockification:** grid items get a block-level computed `display`, so `display: inline` becomes `block` (Chrome reports `"block"`). `height: 30px` and the vertical margins now apply.
- **No margin collapsing:** a grid container creates its own formatting context, and the margins of grid items never collapse, neither with each other nor with the container.

Each implicit `auto` row sizes to its item's margin box: 20 + 30 + 20 = 70px. Two rows give 140px. The first span starts at 20px, and the second at 70 + 20 = 90px. Chrome measures exactly that.

In a grid, use `gap` for spacing between items instead of margins; it never doubles up and doesn't add space at the outer edges.

question: `.row` is 600px wide with a 20px column gap. What happens to its two columns?

options.text: Each column is 300px wide. The second one runs from 320px to 620px, overflowing the container by 20px.
Each column is 290px wide: percentages are resolved against the space left over after the gap.
options.why: That's what `1fr 1fr` does. A percentage track resolves against the container's full content width (600px), whatever the gaps are.

options.text: The second column wraps onto a new row, because 300 + 20 + 300 doesn't fit in 600px.
options.why: Grid never wraps explicit tracks onto a new row. Only `repeat(auto-fill/auto-fit, …)` changes the column count to fit the space. Two fixed columns just overflow.

options.text: The browser shrinks the gap to 0 so the two 50% columns fit exactly.
options.why: Gaps are never reduced to make tracks fit. Chrome's computed `column-gap` stays `20px`, and the second column starts at 320px.

explanation:
A percentage track size resolves against the grid container's content-box width: 50% of 600px = 300px. Gaps are added on top of the tracks: 300 + 20 + 300 = 620px, so the grid overflows by 20px. Chrome reports `grid-template-columns: 300px 300px` and puts the second column at 320–620px.

`fr` works differently: it shares out the space left **after** fixed tracks and gaps are subtracted. With `1fr 1fr`, each column is (600 − 20) / 2 = 290px, and the grid fits exactly. `calc(50% - 10px)` also fits (Chrome measures 290px each).

This comes up when switching from a float or flexbox layout that used `width: 50%` to grid with `gap`: use `fr` and let the grid handle the gutters.

Text blue, prefix blue

explanation:
Specificity, written as (IDs, classes, types):
- `button:enabled::before` → `button` is a type, `:enabled` is a pseudo-class (class column), `::before` is a pseudo-element (type column): **(0,1,2)**.
- `button.btn` → **(0,1,1)**.
- `.btn::before` → **(0,1,1)**.
- `[id="save"]` → an attribute selector counts as a class, even when the attribute is `id`: **(0,1,0)**. Only the `#save` syntax lands in the ID column.

Text: `button.btn` (0,1,1) beats `[id="save"]` (0,1,0), so it is blue. Source order only matters on a tie.

Prefix: `button:enabled::before` (0,1,2) beats `.btn::before` (0,1,1), so it is orange, even though it comes first. The cascade works per property, so the `content: "+ "` from `.btn::before` still applies; only its `color` loses.

Rule of thumb: attribute selectors and pseudo-classes go in the class column, pseudo-elements go in the type column.

question: What color is the "Sale" link? No element on the page has `id="promo"`.

options.text: Red: `:has()` only counts the argument that matched (`> a`), so the green rule is just (0,0,3)
options.why: Like `:is()`, `:has()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument, whether or not that argument is the one that matched. `#promo` makes it (1,0,0), so the green rule is (1,0,2), which beats red (1,0,1).

options.text: Blue: `:not()` and `:has()` each count as one class, so the blue rule's (0,2,1) is highest
options.why: Unlike most pseudo-classes, `:not()` and `:has()` don't count as a class themselves. They are replaced by the specificity of their most specific argument, which here is an ID. Both other rules have an ID column of 1 and beat (0,2,1).

options.text: Blue: `#promo` matches nothing on the page, so it adds no specificity to either rule
options.why: Specificity is computed from the selector text, not from what matches. An ID inside `:not()` or `:has()` counts as an ID even when no element has that id.

options.text: Green: `:has()` takes its most specific argument (`#promo`), making the rule (1,0,2)

explanation:
`:not()` and `:has()` (like `:is()`) have no specificity of their own. Each is replaced by the specificity of the **most specific selector in its argument list**, regardless of which argument matched. Written as (IDs, classes, types):
- `li:has(> a, #promo) a` → `:has()` counts as `#promo` (1,0,0), plus `li` and `a`: **(1,0,2)**.
- `.menu .item a` → **(0,2,1)**.
- `:not(#promo) > a` → `:not()` counts as `#promo` (1,0,0), plus `a`: **(1,0,1)**.

The green rule has the highest specificity, so the link is green even though the red rule comes last.

This is why `:not(#something)` is a heavy selector: the ID inside it counts fully. If you want a negation or a `:has()` test without the weight, wrap it in `:where()`, which is always zero.

topic: Invalid selectors in a selector list
question: Primary buttons used to be dark blue, and keyboard-focused buttons turned dark blue too. A teammate added a third selector for a pressed state, and now **no** button turns dark blue in any state. What happened?

options.text: A selector list only applies when every selector in it matches the element, and nothing ever matches `.btn:pressed`
options.why: A selector list is an OR: the rule applies to elements that match any of the selectors. A valid selector that matches nothing doesn't affect the others. The problem is that `:pressed` isn't valid at all.

options.text: `:pressed` isn't a real pseudo-class, so the whole selector list is invalid and the browser drops the entire rule
Adding a third selector lowers the rule's specificity below `.btn`
options.why: Each selector in a list keeps its own specificity; `.btn.primary` would still be (0,2,0) and beat `.btn` (0,1,0). Specificity isn't the issue: the rule no longer exists in the stylesheet.

options.text: Browsers skip just the `.btn:pressed` part, like an unknown property, so the black must come from a rule elsewhere
options.why: Unknown properties are skipped one declaration at a time, but selectors don't work that way. If any selector in a normal selector list is invalid, the whole rule is thrown away, including the valid `.btn.primary` and `.btn:focus-visible`.

explanation:
CSS error handling treats a selector list as one unit: if any selector in it fails to parse (here the unknown pseudo-class `:pressed`), the **entire rule is dropped**. You can see it in DevTools or `document.styleSheets`: the rule is simply missing, so every button falls back to `.btn { color: black }`.

Fixes:
- Use a real selector for the pressed state, e.g. `.btn:active` or `.btn[aria-pressed="true"]`.
- Put risky selectors (such as new or vendor-prefixed pseudo-classes) in their own rule, so a failure only drops that rule.
- Or wrap the list in `:is()`. It takes a **forgiving** selector list: invalid arguments are ignored and the valid ones keep working. (`:where()` is forgiving too, but its specificity is always zero, so here it would lose to `.btn` and the buttons would stay black.)

```css
:is(.btn.primary, .btn:focus-visible, .btn:pressed) {
  color: darkblue; /* works; :pressed is just ignored */
}
```

Note that `:is()` also changes specificity: every match gets the specificity of the most specific argument, (0,2,0) here.

options.text: Button blue, link green
Button blue, link red

Layer order is set by the **first** time each layer name appears. `components` was already declared by its block above, so the order is `components`, then `base`. The later layer, `base`, wins for normal declarations.

explanation:
The cascade checks **layers before specificity** (and before source order).

**Button:** For normal declarations, unlayered styles sit above all layers. The unlayered `button { color: blue }` beats `#buy.btn` inside `components`, even though `button` is only (0,0,1), the layered rule is (1,1,0), and the unlayered rule comes first in the source.

**Link:** Layer order is fixed by the first time each layer name appears:
- `@layer components { … }` appears first, so `components` is layer 1.
- `@layer base, components;` adds `base` as layer 2. `components` already exists, so it doesn't move.

Later layers beat earlier ones for normal declarations, so `base` wins and the link is green.

To control the order reliably, put a single `@layer a, b, c;` statement at the very top of your CSS, before any layer block.

options.why: Specificity never lets a normal declaration beat an `!important` one. All three `.title` declarations are `!important`, so the `#title` rule loses no matter how specific it is.

options.text: Red

explanation:
`!important` reverses the layer order. The statement `@layer base, theme;` makes `base` the first layer and `theme` the second. Unlayered styles count as an implicit last layer.

From strongest to weakest:
- `!important` in `base` (red)
- `!important` in `theme` (green)
- unlayered `!important` (blue)
- unlayered normal declarations (orange)
- normal declarations in `theme`, then `base`

question: What color is "Hello"?

options.text: Green
Red
options.why: Falling back to an earlier declaration only happens when a declaration is invalid at **parse time** (e.g. `color: 2rem;` written literally). A declaration containing `var()` is assumed valid when parsed, so it wins the cascade and the `red` line is discarded before the variable is ever substituted.

options.text: Blue
options.why: The `var()` fallback is used only when the custom property is missing (or holds the guaranteed-invalid value, e.g. `initial`). `--accent` is defined and inherited from `:root`; its value is just the wrong type for `color`, which doesn't trigger the fallback.

options.text: The initial text color (usually black)
options.why: The declaration does end up acting as `unset`, but `unset` on an inherited property like `color` means `inherit`. So the paragraph takes its parent's green, not the initial value.

explanation:
Step by step:
1. Custom properties inherit, so `.title` sees `--accent: 2rem` from `:root`.
2. At parse time, `color: var(--accent, blue)` can't be checked, so it is accepted. It is the later declaration, so it wins the cascade and `color: red` is gone.
3. At computed-value time, `var(--accent, blue)` becomes `2rem`. The fallback `blue` is **not** used, because `--accent` exists.
4. `2rem` isn't a valid color, so the declaration is **invalid at computed-value time**. The property then behaves as `unset`: for an inherited property like `color` that means `inherit`, so the paragraph takes `.card`'s green.

For a non-inherited property such as `background-color`, the same mistake gives the initial value (`transparent`).

If you need type safety, register the property with `@property --accent { syntax: "<color>"; … }`.

options.text: `.header` forms a stacking context at level 1; the dropdown's 9999 only ranks it inside `.header`, and that whole context paints below `.main` (level 2).
`.main` comes later in the DOM, and later positioned elements always paint over earlier ones.
options.why: Document order only breaks ties between boxes at the same stack level. If `.header` had `z-index: auto`, the dropdown would compete directly at 9999 and cover `.main`, even though `.main` is still later.

options.why: Positioned children overflow their containing block freely unless an ancestor clips them (e.g. `overflow: hidden`). Nothing here clips; the dropdown is drawn, just underneath `.main`.

A positioned element with a `z-index` other than `auto` creates a **stacking context**. Everything inside it is stacked as one unit at the parent's level.

- `.header` → level 1 in the root context
- `.main` → level 2 in the root context
- `.dropdown` → level 9999 **inside** `.header`

question: The header should stay pinned to the top while the page scrolls, but it scrolls away with the content. Only the window scrolls (`body { margin: 0 }`). What's the cause?

options.text: Sticky elements need a positioned parent; `.page` is missing `position: relative`
options.why: That's a rule for `position: absolute`. Sticky doesn't care whether ancestors are positioned. It cares about the nearest ancestor that's a scroll container.

options.text: `overflow-x: hidden` turns `.page` into a scroll container, so the header sticks inside `.page`, which never scrolls
The header needs a `z-index` so it can stay above the scrolling content
options.why: `z-index` only changes painting order. It can fix a sticky header that's covered by other content, but it can't make one stay in place.

options.why: Sticky works at any depth. Change `.page` to `overflow-x: clip` and the same nested header sticks to the viewport.

explanation:
A sticky element sticks relative to its **nearest scrolling ancestor** (the nearest ancestor whose `overflow` is `hidden`, `scroll` or `auto`), not necessarily the viewport.

The trap is that `overflow-x: hidden` also changes the other axis: when one axis is `hidden` and the other is `visible`, the `visible` one computes to `auto` (Chrome reports `overflow-y: auto` for `.page`). So `.page` becomes a scroll container. It has no height limit, so it's as tall as its content and never scrolls itself. The window scrolls instead, carrying `.page` and its "stuck" header away.

Measured in Chrome after `scrollTo(0, 500)`: header top = -500px. If `.page` had a fixed height and scrolled itself, the header would stick inside it.

Fixes:
- Use `overflow-x: clip`. It clips like `hidden` but doesn't create a scroll container, and the header sticks at 0px.
- Or remove the `overflow` from the sticky header's ancestors.

`overflow: hidden` on both axes breaks it the same way.

`overflow: hidden`
options.why: `overflow` doesn't change a fixed element's containing block. With only `overflow: hidden` removed, the toast is still placed against `.card` (its bottom 1184px down the page instead of 784px).

options.text: `position: relative`

A `position: fixed` element is normally positioned against the viewport. - As written, and with any one of `overflow`, `position` or `z-index` removed: the toast's bottom is 1184px down the page (scroll 0) and 284px from the viewport top (scroll 900). It's attached to the card.

Both are 200px wide
options.why: That's only true for `.b`. The default is `box-sizing: content-box`, where `width` sets the content area alone, so `.a`'s padding and border are added on top: 200 + 40 + 10 = 250px.

`display: flex; flex-direction: column;`
options.why: This does fix it. Margins of flex items never collapse with the flex container's margins, so the heading's margin stays inside the card.

explanation:
A parent's top margin and its first in-flow child's top margin are **adjoining** when nothing separates them: no top border, no top padding, no clearance, and the parent doesn't establish a new formatting context. Adjoining margins collapse into one margin, and that combined margin sits **outside** the parent. So the card itself is pushed 24px down from the banner, and its background starts at the heading.

`position: relative` only lets you offset the box visually. It doesn't create a block formatting context, so the margins still collapse (Chrome still shows a 24px gap above the card and the heading at the card's top edge).

What does stop it:

- Top `padding` or `border` on the parent.
- `display: flow-root` (or `overflow: hidden`/`auto`, which also create a BFC but clip).
- Making the parent a flex or grid container.

Note that `min-height` doesn't help with the top margin either; in Chrome the gap stays above the card.

question: `.spacer` is completely empty: no content, no padding, no border, and no height. How far is the bottom of `.a` from the top of `.b`?

options.text: 20px: an empty block's margins are ignored, so only `.a`'s and `.b`'s margins collapse.
options.why: The spacer's margins aren't ignored. They join the collapse, and its 30px top margin is the largest of the four, so it decides the gap.

options.text: 30px
45px: 30px above the spacer (20 vs 30) plus 15px below it (10 vs 15).
options.why: That's roughly what happens once the spacer has any height, padding or border to keep its two margins apart (with `height: 1px`, Chrome gives 30 + 1 + 15 = 46px). An empty block has nothing between its margins, so they collapse through it.
This adds every margin. Adjoining vertical margins between blocks collapse instead of adding up.

explanation:
If a block has zero height, no padding, no border, no content (no line boxes) and `min-height: 0`, its own top and bottom margins are adjoining, and they collapse **through** the box. The spacer's margins then also adjoin `.a`'s bottom margin and `.b`'s top margin, so all four collapse into one margin: max(20, 30, 10, 15) = **30px**. Chrome measures exactly 30px.

As soon as the spacer has something between its margins (`height: 1px`, `padding-top: 1px`, or a 1px `border-top`), the top pair and the bottom pair collapse separately, and the gap jumps to 46px.

Empty spacer elements are a fragile way to make space. Margins on the real content, or `gap` in a flex or grid container, are more predictable.

question: Both images are floated, and the gallery's border shrinks to a 4px line above them instead of wrapping around them. Which change to `.gallery` makes the border wrap around the images? Default UA styles otherwise.

snippets.code:
.gallery { border: 2px solid; }
.gallery img { float: left; width: 100px; height: 100px; }

options.text: `display: flow-root;`
`clear: both;`
options.why: `clear` on an element moves that element below floats that come **before** it. It does nothing about floats **inside** it. The gallery stays 4px tall.

options.text: `height: 100%;`
options.why: The gallery's parent (`body`) has `height: auto`, so the percentage behaves as `auto` and the gallery stays 4px tall. Even a resolved height would be a fixed size, not one that follows the floats.

options.text: `position: relative;`
options.why: Relative positioning doesn't create a block formatting context, so the floats still don't count toward the gallery's height. It stays 4px tall.

explanation:
Floats are taken out of normal flow. A normal block's `auto` height only counts its in-flow content, so the gallery's content height is 0 and you only see its 2px top and bottom borders.

A box that establishes a **block formatting context** (BFC) includes the floats inside it when computing its `auto` height. `display: flow-root` exists for exactly this: it creates a BFC with no side effects, and the gallery becomes 104px tall (100px images + 4px of border, checked in Chrome).

Other ways to get the same result:

- `overflow: hidden` or `overflow: auto` also create a BFC, but they clip or scroll anything that sticks out.
- The older clearfix adds a cleared block after the floats:

```css
.gallery::after { content: ""; display: block; clear: both; }
```

question: `.viewport` clips its 300px-tall content with `overflow: hidden`. What does the script log, and what happens on screen?

options.text: `0 300`: `overflow: hidden` turns scrolling off, so the assignment is ignored.
options.why: That's the behavior of `overflow: clip`, which clips without making a scroll container (Chrome logs `0 300` for it). `hidden` only hides the scrollbars; the box is still a scroll container.

options.text: `50 100`: it scrolls, but `scrollHeight` only counts the visible part.
options.why: `scrollHeight` measures all of the content, including the clipped part. It's 300 here, not the 100px visible height.

options.text: `50 300`, and the content moves up 50px inside the viewport
`50 300`, but nothing moves on screen, because hidden overflow is never painted.
options.why: The scroll offset is real. After the assignment, the content's top edge is 50px above the viewport's top edge, so a different slice of it is visible.

explanation:
`overflow: hidden` clips the content and shows no scrollbars, but the element is still a **scroll container**. Scripts can scroll it with `scrollTop`, `scrollTo()` or `scrollIntoView()` on a descendant. In Chrome, `vp.scrollTop` reads back `50`, `scrollHeight` is `300`, and the content's top edge moves to 50px above the viewport's top.

`overflow: clip` is the value that clips **without** creating a scroll container. With it, the same script logs `0 300` and nothing moves. Use `clip` when you want clipping with no scrolling at all, not even from script.
